title: The history of understanding squid
tagline: 2,350 years from Aristotle’s ink sacs to the nerve that explained every nerve and mirrors built from squid protein.
intro: People have eaten and wondered about squid since ancient times. In the twentieth century the squid’s giant nerve fibre taught us how nerves fire, its glowing bacteria taught us how microbes talk, and its tunable skin mirrors are now teaching engineers how to make new materials.

eras.name: First looks
eras.summary: Ancient writers describe squid, their fins and their ink.

eras.name: The giant nerve
eras.summary: The squid giant axon is found and used to work out how every nerve fires.

eras.name: Living light and partners
eras.summary: Glowing bacteria reveal quorum sensing, and the bobtail squid becomes a model partnership.

eras.name: Tunable mirrors, materials and fisheries
eras.summary: Reflectin is found and its tuning explained, materials copy it, and India sets rules for its squid fishery.

events.title: Two kinds of squid, and their ink
events.text: In his History of Animals, Aristotle described a small squid and a much bigger one, and how their fins differ. He placed the ink sac under the mouth and wrote that squid, octopus and cuttlefish all squirt ink when alarmed, the cuttlefish most of all.
events.why: It is the oldest careful written account of squid and their ink.

events.title: The giant nerve fibre is found
events.text: Studying squid nerves, the zoologist John Zachary Young saw that pale cords on the mantle, thick enough to see by eye, were single enormous nerve fibres running from the stellate ganglion.
events.why: A nerve fibre this big could be studied from the inside.

events.title: Bigger fibres for longer trips
events.who: R. J. Pumphrey and J. Z. Young
events.text: Measuring squid and cuttlefish nerves, they showed that thicker fibres conduct faster, and that the larger giant fibres are the ones that run the greater distances over the mantle.
events.why: It explained how one signal can squeeze the whole mantle at once.

events.title: A nerve signal recorded from inside
events.text: They threaded a fine electrode along the inside of a squid giant axon about half a millimetre wide. During a signal the inside swung from about −45 to about +40 millivolts: it did not just switch off, it flipped.
events.why: It was the first recording of a nerve impulse from inside a nerve fibre.

events.title: Holding the voltage still
events.text: Working on squid giant axons, Cole and Marmont built the voltage clamp, a circuit that holds the voltage across the nerve membrane fixed so the currents flowing through it can be measured.
events.why: Hodgkin and Huxley used the method to measure the sodium and potassium currents.

events.title: How a nerve fires, worked out
events.text: In a series of papers using squid giant axons, they showed how sodium rushing in and potassium flowing out make the nerve spike, and wrote equations that predicted its shape and speed.
events.why: Their model still underlies how we understand every nerve and neuron.

events.title: Ink as a decoy
events.text: In a letter to Nature, Hall argued that cephalopod ink is not just a black smokescreen: blobs of ink can work as decoys that draw a predator’s attack.
events.why: It started the study of ink pseudomorphs, the squid’s inky doubles.

events.title: A Nobel Prize for the squid’s nerve
events.who: Alan Hodgkin, Andrew Huxley and John Eccles
events.text: Hodgkin and Huxley shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Eccles for discoveries about how nerve cell membranes carry signals.
events.why: It recognised work built on the squid giant axon.

events.title: Bacteria that glow only in a crowd
events.who: Kenneth Nealson, Terry Platt and J. Woodland Hastings
events.text: They found that the glowing bacterium Vibrio fischeri only turns on its light once a culture is dense, because each cell leaks a signal that builds up. Hastings called it autoinduction; today it is called quorum sensing.
events.why: Quorum sensing is now known in many bacteria, including ones that cause disease.

events.title: The bobtail squid becomes a model
events.text: McFall-Ngai and Ruby showed that a newly hatched Hawaiian bobtail squid picks up Vibrio fischeri from sea water and that the bacteria reshape its light organ. The pair became a model for how animals and helpful microbes find each other (date as given in reviews, attributed).
events.why: It made the squid a key animal for studying partnerships between hosts and microbes.

events.title: Blanch, ink, jet
events.text: In their book Cephalopod Behaviour they described the squid’s escape sequence: turn pale, release a decoy blob of ink, then jet away. They called it the blanch–ink–jet manoeuvre.
events.why: It tied colour change, ink and jetting together into one escape.

events.title: A daily clear-out at dawn
events.text: They reported that each dawn the bobtail squid vents about 90% of its light-organ bacteria into the sea; later studies give about 95%. The rest regrow during the day.
events.why: It showed the squid controls its glowing partners on a daily rhythm.

events.title: Glowing to hide a shadow, tested
events.text: In the lab they showed that the light coming from the bobtail squid’s light organ rises and falls as the light from above changes. That is counter-illumination: glowing on the belly to erase its shadow.
events.why: It was the first direct lab test that the squid uses its bacteria for camouflage.

events.title: Reflectins are named
events.text: Studying the reflective tissues of squid, the team described a new family of proteins, unlike any known before, that build the reflecting plates. They called them reflectins.
events.why: Reflectin is the key to the squid’s tunable mirrors.

events.title: A decoy that works
events.where: Caribbean reef squid, in the lab
events.text: Experiments with Caribbean reef squid showed that an ink pseudomorph delays a predatory fish from catching its food, by blocking what it can see and smell.
events.why: It gave evidence that ink decoys really help squid escape.

events.title: Nerves tune the mirrors
events.who: Trevor Wardill, Paloma Gonzalez-Bellido, Robyn Crook and Roger Hanlon
events.text: Stimulating skin nerves of the longfin squid switched on its iridophores: the colour shifted from red toward blue in about 17 seconds and the brightness rose over about half a minute.
events.why: It was the first proof that nerves control iridescence in an invertebrate.

events.title: Squeezing water out of the plates
events.who: Daniel DeMartini, Daniel Krogstad and Daniel Morse
events.text: They showed that acetylcholine makes reflectin condense, and water flows out of the plates through folds in the cell’s membrane. The plates thin and the reflected colour changes; when the signal goes, water flows back.
events.why: It explained how a squid can tune a mirror made of living cells.

events.title: Measuring the living mirrors
events.who: Amitabh Ghoshal, Daniel DeMartini, Elizabeth Eck and Daniel Morse
events.text: Measuring single stacks in live market squid, they found the plates thin from about 150 to 80 nm and the gaps from about 120 to 50 nm to tune the colour from 675 nm red to 425 nm blue, with eight or nine plate pairs reflecting.
events.why: These are the numbers behind the model in this box.

events.title: Squid that fly
events.who: Kouta Muramatsu, Jun Yamamoto and colleagues
events.text: From a training ship, scientists photographed a shoal of small ocean squid jetting out of the water and gliding on their fins and arms, reported as up to about 30 metres at up to about 11 metres a second.
events.why: It confirmed that some squid really fly through the air to escape.

events.title: India bans LED light fishing at sea
events.who: Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries
events.text: An order banned bull and pair trawling and the use of artificial and LED lights by mechanised and motorised fishing craft in India’s Exclusive Economic Zone, from 12 to 200 nautical miles out. Traditional non-motorised craft are exempt.
events.why: Strong lights pull in young fish as well as squid, and small-boat fishers had asked for limits.

events.title: Infrared camouflage from squid ideas
events.who: Chengyi Xu, Alon Gorodetsky and colleagues
events.text: Inspired by cephalopod skin, the team made thin, stretchable films that change how much heat they reflect, so a warm object can be hidden from infrared cameras (Science, 2018).
events.why: It showed how squid-like tunable reflectors could become real materials.

events.title: A big squid stock in the Arabian Sea
events.text: A survey of the purpleback flying squid estimated an average of about 4.2 tonnes per square kilometre and a sustainable catch of about 0.63 million tonnes a year in the area, enough, the authors said, for a new oceanic squid fishery (estimate from the study’s abstract).
events.why: It points to a large squid resource India hardly uses.

events.title: Backlit signals in the deep
events.where: Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute and Stanford
events.text: Filming 30 Humboldt squid 266 to 848 metres deep, they found the squid show set patterns while hunting and meeting others, and suggested lights in their muscle backlight the patterns so they can be read in the dark.
events.why: It hinted that squid may hold complex conversations in the dark.

events.title: Human cells with squid protein
events.who: Atrouli Chatterjee, Alon Gorodetsky and colleagues
events.text: The team made human cells produce reflectin. The cells formed tiny protein particles and changed how much light they scattered when the salt around them changed.
events.why: It showed a squid trick working inside human cells.

events.title: Cephalopods recognised as sentient
events.text: After an independent review of the evidence, the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 recognised cephalopods, including squid, and decapod crustaceans as sentient animals.
events.why: It means UK policies must consider how they affect squid welfare.

events.title: India’s cephalopod catch
events.text: CMFRI estimated that India landed about 2.13 lakh tonnes of cephalopods in 2023, about 6% of its marine catch and its fourth-largest group. Squid are roughly half; the main species is the Indian squid.
events.why: It shows how important squid are to India’s fishers.

events.title: Frozen squid among the top exports
events.text: For 2023–24, MPEDA reported frozen squid as India’s fourth-largest seafood export item, worth about ₹3,061 crore (US$373 million) and about 5% of exports by quantity.
events.why: Squid earns India hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

facts: A squid’s shimmering colours come from stacks of protein plates about a tenth of a micrometre thick, not from pigment.
A nerve signal can slide a squid iridophore’s colour from red to blue in about 17 seconds.
Each dawn the Hawaiian bobtail squid squirts about 90 to 95% of its glowing bacteria into the sea.
The squid giant axon is about half a millimetre thick, big enough to slide a wire inside.
India landed about 2.13 lakh tonnes of cephalopods in 2023.
